claims.text: A two-channel ab-initio framework can independently compute lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The framework will accurately treat both pristine HfNbTaTiZr and material containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The lattice channel will be calculated from DFT phonon dispersions, anharmonic and oxygen-defect scattering rates, and the phonon Boltzmann transport equation.
The electronic channel will be calculated from electronic band structures and scattering times associated with disorder and electron-phonon coupling.
Atomic-scale disorder and oxygen-induced point defects modify local force constants.
Atomic-scale disorder and oxygen-induced point defects alter electronic scattering channels.
Separately treating phonon and electronic scattering isolates the two carrier spectra and avoids conflating lattice and electronic conductivity.
Nonlinear electron-phonon or defect-related coupling may require sensitivity analysis or correction near 200–300 K.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are nearly equal or comparable.
An HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen has a measured total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) between 300 and 1200 K.
The separate lattice-conductivity prediction will be approximately 10–15% more accurate than earlier single-channel analytical approaches.
Predicted total conductivity will agree with high-temperature measurements within ±5 W/(K m).
Earlier approaches used an effective Debye temperature and idealized defect-free models.
Earlier approaches conflated lattice and electronic conductivity and inadequately represented atomic-scale disorder and defects.
The proposed framework is limited to pristine HfNbTaTiZr or specimens containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen over roughly 50–1300 K.
A lattice-conductivity deviation greater than 10–15% at low temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
A total-conductivity deviation greater than ±5 W/(K m) from measurements between 300 and 1200 K would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reproduce nearly equal lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K would falsify the hypothesis.
